newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea state think-tank lowers economic forecasts.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea state think-tank lowers economic forecasts.

text.p: Amid an atmosphere of increasing anxiety over the economy and job security, a key state think-tank on Thursday joined the chorus of forecasters lowering their estimates of South Korea's GDP growth this year.

Citing shrinking private and government spending and falling corporate capital investment, the Korea Development Institute said it now estimated the country's real GDP would rise by 6.0 percent in 1997, compared to an earlier forecast of 6.4 percent.
"Private spending is quickly falling due to jitters about job security and gloomy economic prospects," said Kim Joon-kyung, a fellow at the Korea Development Insitute (KDI).
Last week the central Bank of Korea lowered its GDP growth forecast to 5.5-6.0 percent from 6.4 percent, while the government earlier pared its forecast to 5.5 percent from 6.0 percent.
The nation's GDP rose by 7.1 percent in 1996, down from 8.9 percent growth in 1995 and an 8.6 percent rise in 1994.

While countries like the United States and Japan would find 6 percent growth something to cheer, newly industrializing Korea is accustomed to double-digit growth. Economists also have voiced concern about the rapid slowdown of Korea's growth.
Capital investment -- spending on machinery and other industrial facilities -- is predicted to decline 4.5 percent this year, against an 8.2 percent increase in 1996, KDI said.
KDI predicted this year's private spending would grow by 5.2 percent, against a 6.9 percent rise in 1996, and that government spending would increase 2.8 percent versus 7.1 percent in 1996.
"The growing jobless rate made consumers realise how serious the current situation is. So they are spending less," said Lee Hahn-koo, president of the private Daewoo Research Institute.
South Korea's jobless rate before taking seasonal factors into account rose to a three-year high of 3.2 percent in February from 2.3 percent a year earlier.
"Companies will inevitably feel the need to readjust their workforce as the final phase of a restructuring," said Lee.
Moreover, major business conglomerates have announced plans to freeze or cut fresh employment to match slowing sales growth and falling profit margins.
The government has pledged to slash this year's budget spending by two trillion won ($2.2 billion) to take the lead in a belt-tightening campaign.
Meanwhile, KDI raised its forecast for the current account deficit to $19.6 billion from $15.5 billion, compared with the Bank of Korea's forecast for a deficit of just over $18 billion.
Last year, the current account deficit rose to a record $23.72 billion from an $8.95 billion shortfall in 1995.

"The current account deficit is expected to improve from the second half, helped by recovering exports," said KDI's Kim. "A recovery in memory chip prices over late last year will also help support the nation's exports."

Last year's 80-percent decline in prices of 16-megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips has generally been blamed for the snowballing current account deficit. Memory chips account for about 20 percent of South Korea's exports.
Recently, the per-unit price of 16-megabit DRAM chips has stood at about $12 in international spot markets, up from about $6 late last year.
Analysts said the recent sharp depreciation of the Korean won against the U.S. dollar would also begin paying off and boost exports by making South Korean products cheaper.
The won lost about six percent to the greenback this year on top of an eight percent drop, due largely to the nation's huge current account deficit and the weakness of the Japanese yen.
The won now stands at 894 per dollar, compared with 844 won at the end of 1996.
